The rain had cancelled the school picnic, and the power was out in the whole lane. Shalini, nine, sat by the window with her uncle's old college physics book, working out why raindrops fall at the speed they do. It was more fun than her Class 4 sums, which she finished in five minutes and then sat bored.
But when her drawing of the rain came out wobbly, she tore it up and cried. "It has to be perfect."
Her mother sat beside her and held her. "It doesn't. You're nine." Then she looked at the physics book and closed it gently. "Enough big-person reading. Darshan is splashing in the puddles outside. Go."
Shalini hesitated, then ran out barefoot. Ten minutes later she was soaked, shrieking, racing paper boats with Darshan down the drain.

qa.q: What was Shalini reading by the window?
qa.a: Her uncle's old college physics book.

qa.q: Why did Shalini tear up her drawing and cry?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and upset because it wasn't perfect, and she expects everything she does to be flawless.

qa.q: What did Shalini's mother do that nurtured the whole child?
qa.a: She comforted her, told her she didn't need to be perfect, and sent her out to play with Darshan instead of praising only the physics.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Shalini racing paper boats with him?
qa.a: Darshan probably just sees a fun friend to play with in the rain, not a brainy girl who is different.

grounding: Shalini understands physics far above her age yet still needs play and comfort, and her mother nurtures the whole child through her perfectionism and boredom.

"Done, Ma'am."
"Mohit, I gave those sums four minutes ago."
"They were easy. Ma'am, why can't you divide by zero? What would happen?"
Kiran Ma'am paused. "Good question. Let's talk after—"
But by the time she had checked three notebooks, Mohit was flicking paper balls at Arjun and humming.
After class, Kiran Ma'am called him over. "Mohit, you're disturbing others."
"I'm bored, Ma'am. Should I just do more sums?"
"No. More sums won't help you. Here's something harder. Find three different ways to explain why dividing by zero doesn't work. You can use drawings, stories, anything. Show me on Friday."
Mohit's eyes widened. "Anything?"
"Anything. And bring me your next question too. I like your questions."
On Friday he brought four explanations and a new question about infinity.

qa.q: How many explanations did Mohit bring on Friday?
qa.a: He brought four explanations and a new question about infinity.

qa.q: What was Kiran Ma'am feeling when she told Mohit she liked his questions?
qa.a: She felt genuine interest and admiration for his curious mind, even though his disruption had annoyed her.

qa.q: Why did Kiran Ma'am's task work better than extra sums?
qa.a: It gave Mohit deeper, open-ended thinking instead of more of the same work, and respected his questions, so his interest stayed alive.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel when told he could use anything to explain?
qa.a: He likely felt excited and valued, as if his curiosity was finally welcome in class.

grounding: Kiran Ma'am sees a bright pupil finish early, ask probing questions and then disrupt, and keeps his interest alive with depth and respect for his questions.

Dear Bidisha Didi,
You asked in your last email how Class 10 is going. Honestly? Lonely. At lunch everyone talks about the same show, and when I mention the black hole paper I read, they look at me like I'm from another planet. So I've started pretending I didn't understand the maths homework either, just to fit in.
And then there's the other thing. Papa pins every rank card on the fridge. When I came second in chemistry, I couldn't sleep.
But something good happened. Ms Rao sent me to the district astronomy club. There are kids there who argue about telescopes for hours. I felt normal for the first time in months.
And Ms Rao said something I keep repeating: "You're allowed to be average at some things." It felt like putting down a school bag.
Write back soon,
Sangeeta

qa.q: Where did Ms Rao send Sangeeta?
qa.a: To the district astronomy club.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel at lunch with classmates?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt lonely and out of step, so much so that pretending not to understand the homework seemed the only way to fit in.

qa.q: What helped relieve the pressure, and why?
qa.a: Finding like-minded kids at the astronomy club and a mentor's permission to be average sometimes, which eased the need to be top in everything.

qa.q: How might Bidisha Didi feel reading this email?
qa.a: Bidisha Didi might feel concerned about the loneliness and sleepless night, and relieved that Sangeeta has found a place to feel normal.

grounding: Sangeeta feels out of step, hides ability to belong and feels every result must be top, until like-minded peers and a mentor's permission to be average relieve the strain.

passage:
Mum: Physics result? 🤔
Sachin: 92
Mum: What happened to the other 8? Riya's son got 99. You're capable of more.
Sachin: ok
Mum: We'll add Sunday tuition.
Sachin: Mum can I ask something
Mum: Yes
Sachin: Would you still be proud of me if I was just normal? Like 70s?
Sachin: Sometimes it feels like you only like me when I top.
Mum: ...
Mum: Sachin, that's not true. But I can see why it feels that way.
Mum: I'm sorry. I love you for you. Your jokes, how you help Nani with her phone, all of it.
Sachin: really?
Mum: Really. 92 is great. No Sunday tuition. Let's get chaat tonight.
Sachin: ok. thanks Mum

qa.q: Whose son got 99, according to Mum?
qa.a: Riya's son.

qa.q: How was Sachin feeling when asking if Mum would still be proud with marks in the 70s?
qa.a: Sachin felt hurt and anxious, as if Mum's love depended on being brilliant.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what did Mum do to fix it?
qa.a: Her pressure made Sachin feel loved only for marks; she apologised, named things she loves about Sachin beyond ability and dropped the extra tuition.

qa.q: How might Mum be feeling after reading Sachin's question?
qa.a: She seems shocked and guilty, then tender, realising her pride had come across as conditional love.

grounding: Sachin feels loved only for brilliance because of Mum's push for achievement, and her valuing Sachin beyond ability brings reassurance.

Dear Professor Sharmila,
I wanted to explain the late submission and what happened in the group meeting.
You've said my analysis of the survey data was the best in the cohort. I believe the numbers part is strong. But I lost the final draft twice because my files are everywhere, and I missed two deadlines this term.
Then, when Kunal disagreed with my model, I said his idea was "obviously wrong" in front of everyone. I didn't notice he was upset until he left. I felt so ashamed that I skipped the next meeting.
I've been thinking. Maybe I'm not "brilliant but careless". Maybe I'm strong at analysis and still learning organisation and how people hear me. I've started a weekly file check and I apologised to Kunal.
Could I meet you to plan the rest of the project?
Irawati

qa.q: How many deadlines did Irawati miss this term?
qa.a: Two deadlines.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel after noticing Kunal was upset?
qa.a: Irawati felt deeply ashamed, so much that the next meeting was skipped.

qa.q: What change in thinking helps Irawati work on the gaps?
qa.a: Seeing strengths and gaps without shame, so Irawati can keep the analysis skills while practising organisation and how words land.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt in the meeting?
qa.a: He was likely hurt and embarrassed to have his idea called obviously wrong in front of everyone.

grounding: Irawati, brilliant at analysis but struggling with organisation and social skills, learns to see strengths and gaps without shame and works on each.

passage:
Hemant ran across the cowshed yard in Ambajogai, dust flying. "D-d-d-Didi! The c-c-c-calf! It's b-b-born!" His face squeezed tight on the hard sounds, but he didn't seem to notice.
Ira, his big sister, put down the water pot and turned to him. She didn't finish his words or tell him to slow down. She just looked at him and waited, smiling.
"It's b-brown and w-w-wobbly!"
"Brown and wobbly! Show me."
Hemant grabbed her hand and pulled her towards the shed, still chattering.

qa.q: What was the calf like, according to Hemant?
qa.a: Brown and wobbly.

qa.q: How was Hemant feeling as he ran across the yard?
qa.a: He was very excited about the new calf, so excited he didn't notice his face squeezing on the hard sounds.

qa.q: What did Ira do that helps a child who repeats sounds?
qa.a: She stayed calm, looked at him and waited without finishing his words or telling him to slow down.

qa.q: What would change if Ira had said "Say it properly"?
qa.a: Hemant might have felt embarrassed and noticed his speech, and his excitement could have turned into worry about talking.

grounding: Hemant repeats sounds with tension in his face when excited, seemingly unaware, and his sister listens calmly without finishing his words.

In the colony park in Nagpur, Vijay was trying to tell Sachin about his new kite. "It's a b-b-b..." His eyes squeezed.
"Say it fast!" called another boy from the swings.
Sachin didn't. He held the ball against his tummy and kept looking at Vijay, waiting.
"...b-big red one with a t-tail."
"A tail! How long?" Sachin asked.
Vijay stretched his arms wide and grinned. They talked about the kite until Sachin's Nani called him home.

qa.q: What colour is Vijay's new kite?
qa.a: It's a big red one with a tail.

qa.q: Why did Sachin keep holding the ball and looking at Vijay?
qa.a: He was curious and interested in the kite and patient enough to wait for Vijay to finish.

qa.q: Which choice worked better, Sachin's or the boy on the swings, and why?
qa.a: Sachin's, because waiting and asking a real question treated Vijay as a full conversation partner, while "Say it fast" added pressure.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel when Sachin asks how long the tail is?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and happy that Sachin cares about his kite, not about how he said it.

grounding: Sachin waits for Vijay's stuttered words without finishing them or rushing him, treating him as a full conversation partner.

Tuesday. Jaya's stomach knotted as the reading round moved down the row. She said "I feel sick" and went to the washroom before her turn. When she had to answer the attendance, she said "present" instead of "yes, Ma'am" because "y" often got stuck.
Friday. Saurabh copied her in the corridor: "P-p-present!" Jaya didn't speak in class at all that day.
The next Wednesday. Mrs Dutta, the class teacher, had spoken to Saurabh, and he said sorry. She told Jaya she could read in her own time, with no rushing and no one finishing words. Jaya also had her first session with a speech therapist at the city hospital. That afternoon she read two lines aloud. It was slow. Nobody laughed.

qa.q: What did Jaya say instead of "yes, Ma'am" at attendance?
qa.a: She said "present".

qa.q: How did Jaya feel as the reading round moved down the row?
qa.a: She felt afraid and dreaded her turn, with her stomach knotting so she made an excuse to leave.

qa.q: What helped Jaya read aloud again?
qa.a: The teacher stopped the teasing, gave her time without rushing, and she began sessions with a speech therapist.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see things differently after Mrs Dutta spoke to him?
qa.a: He may realise his copying hurt Jaya and made speaking even harder for her.

grounding: Jaya avoids reading aloud, swaps words and dreads being called on; teasing makes it worse, and teacher patience plus a speech therapist help.

Class teacher's note, Mrs Nirmala Iyer, Class 9B.
Tanvir scored highest in the written history test, but in class he hardly speaks. I've seen him writing answers in the margin before I finish asking, lips moving, rehearsing. When the office asked him to phone his father about a late pickup, he stood by the phone for five minutes and then asked a friend to call.
Today, when he tried to answer, he got stuck on "Mughal" and two boys smirked. He went red and looked down for the rest of the period.
After class, I spoke to him alone. I told him his answers were some of the best in the class and that I would stop any smirking. I offered written or one-to-one answers when he wanted. I've also called his parents to discuss the school counsellor and a speech therapist.

qa.q: Which word did Tanvir get stuck on today?
qa.a: He got stuck on "Mughal".

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel when the two boys smirked?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and embarrassed, going red and looking down for the rest of the period.

qa.q: What did Mrs Iyer do next that could reduce Tanvir's stress?
qa.a: She praised his ideas, promised to stop the smirking, offered written or one-to-one answers and spoke to his parents about a counsellor and a speech therapist.

qa.q: How might the smirking boys' reaction affect Tanvir more than the stuck word itself?
qa.a: Their reaction is what made him hide, so it adds more stress than the speech itself, since his thoughts were clear and ready.

grounding: A teacher notices Tanvir's clear thoughts, silence, avoided phone calls and rehearsing, and that his shame comes more from others' reactions than from speech.

The seminar room at the Chennai college was full when Vidya stood up to present. "Before I start," she said, "I stutter. Some words take longer. I'll get there."
She spoke slowly. On "p-p-population" she paused, breathed and carried on. She didn't say sorry once.
In the front row, Payal kept her eyes on Vidya's face and nodded, waiting. The professor didn't rush her either.
At the end, a student asked a sharp question about her data, and Vidya answered it fully. Afterwards Payal said, "That was brilliant."
"Two years ago I'd have skipped this," Vidya admitted. "I felt like the only person in the world who talked like me. Then I found a Saturday support group for people who stutter. Turns out, I wasn't alone."

qa.q: What does Vidya go to on Saturdays?
qa.a: A support group for people who stutter.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel two years ago?
qa.a: She felt lonely and isolated, like the only person in the world who talked like her.

qa.q: What helped Vidya present with confidence?
qa.a: Naming her stutter openly, slowing down without apologising, patient listeners who kept eye contact, and the support group that made her feel less alone.

qa.q: How does Payal see Vidya's presentation?
qa.a: She admires it and calls it brilliant, focusing on Vidya's ideas rather than the pauses.

grounding: Vidya speaks openly about her stutter, slows down without apologising, is helped by patient listeners, and a support group eased her isolation.
